WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Throughout her career, singer-songwriter Cyndi Lauper has promoted gay and lesbian rights. She has a personal connection to this cause -- her sister is a lesbian -- but she also believes it's a matter of fairness. Cyndi Lauper worked with Cathy Nelson of the Human Rights Campaign to raise awareness of LGBT issues. "It's always wrong to discriminate," the Grammy Award winner said. "I grew up in the civil rights movement. It was wrong then, and it is wrong now." With her 2007 and 2008 "True Colors" tours, Lauper has helped raise awareness about lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender rights around the country. She said fellow LGBT activist Cathy Nelson especially motivates her. Nelson worked at the Human Rights Campaign (HRC), a national LGBT civil rights organization, and her dedication to those issues runs deep. Fighting for fairness and equality, she said, drives her. "I'm a lesbian, and I see the issues very personally," Nelson said. "When it deep-down resonates that you don't have the same rights and responsibilities, or people don't view you the same, it can be demoralizing and empowering at the same time." Nelson's passion for the cause has enabled her to inspire thousands of people across the country to get involved. When she was growing up in rural Illinois, Nelson said, she hadn't imagined following this path. She trained to be a teacher, but on a whim, became a flight attendant with Eastern Airlines to fulfill her "intense desire to travel." In the 1980s, she became involved with labor issues through her flight attendant union. That led to working on women's issues with the National Organization of Women in Washington. In 1989, she started working for the HRC. Since then, she has helped bring LGBT rights out of the closet and onto the national stage. Hired to increase the group's membership, Nelson built a strong volunteer network in communities across the nation. HRC had just 12,000 members when Nelson started. Today it has more than 725,000, making it the largest gay and lesbian rights organization in the country. "Part of my job is getting people to be vocal," Nelson said. "It's important that everyone has an understanding that discrimination is happening every single day against a certain segment of society. And that's just wrong." In 2007, when Lauper worked with HRC for the "True Colors" tour, she and Nelson teamed up to bring gay and straight audiences together on fairness and equality issues. Nelson realized it was also an opportunity to shine the spotlight on an issue she'd worked on for almost a decade -- the passage of a hate crimes bill that would make attacks based on sexual orientation, disability, or gender a federal crime. For Nelson, crimes against LGBT people -- such as the murder of Matthew Shepard -- represent the darkest side of ignorance on these issues. In 2006, more than one in six hate crimes were committed against LGBT individuals, an 18 percent rise over the previous year, according to the FBI. "I learned from Cathy that hate crimes send fear through a community," Lauper said. "You could die just because of who you are."  Watch Lauper and Nelson talk about the "True Colors" tour to raise awareness » . At every concert, Lauper spoke passionately about the need to pass the bill, and her song, "True Colors," was used in a public service announcement about the legislation. HRC volunteers distributed information at each venue and had postcards on hand for people to send to their legislators. In the end, more than 15,000 people signed postcards, and both houses of Congress passed the bill by wide margins. Although President Bush never signed the bill, Nelson and Lauper have high hopes for it to soon become law. For Nelson, getting so many people engaged was a key achievement. "The biggest reward for me is when I've played some part in empowering someone to get involved," she said. Lauper knows first-hand how convincing Nelson can be. "The fact that you can actually succeed and help people -- you really get that from her," she said. "People like Cathy get all of us motivated."

Nelson’s dedication has helped encourage thousands of people nationwide to take action. But while growing up in rural Illinois, she said she never expected her life to follow that course. She studied to become a teacher, then unexpectedly took a job as a flight attendant with Eastern Airlines because of what she described as a strong urge to travel.

During the 1980s, Nelson became active in labor matters through the flight attendants’ union. That experience later brought her to Washington, where she worked on women’s issues with the National Organization for Women. In 1989, she joined HRC.

Since that time, Nelson has played a role in moving LGBT rights from the margins into national public debate. Initially hired to expand HRC’s membership, she created a powerful network of volunteers in communities around the United States.

“A big part of what I do is encourage people to speak up,” Nelson said. “People need to understand that discrimination is taking place every day against a specific group in society. And that is simply wrong.”

## “True Colors” in Action: How Cyndi Lauper and Cathy Nelson Helped Bring LGBT Rights Into the Spotlight

Long before corporate Pride campaigns became common and mainstream pop stars routinely spoke out for equality, Cyndi Lauper was using her voice to defend gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people. Best known to many as the singer of joyful, era-defining hits such as “Girls Just Want to Have Fun” and “True Colors,” Lauper turned one of her most beloved songs into something larger than music: a public call for dignity, safety and equal rights.

A key part of that work came through her partnership with activist and organizer Cathy Nelson, whose background in advocacy helped connect Lauper’s celebrity platform with national LGBT rights campaigns. Together, they helped raise awareness at a crucial moment for the movement, including efforts to pass federal hate crimes protections and the launch of the True Colors tour.

### Turning a pop anthem into a civil rights message

“True Colors,” released in 1986, became an unofficial anthem for many LGBT people because of its message of acceptance and visibility. Lauper recognized that connection and embraced it. Rather than distancing herself from the community that had supported her from the beginning, she leaned in, speaking openly about equality and using concerts, media appearances and public campaigns to challenge discrimination.

Cathy Nelson helped shape that energy into organized activism. Their collaboration was rooted in a simple idea: music could open doors that politics alone often could not. A concert could bring people together emotionally, but it could also direct them toward action—signing petitions, contacting lawmakers, supporting advocacy organizations and learning about the real-life consequences of anti-LGBT bias.

### The hate crimes bill campaign

One of the major issues Lauper and Nelson helped elevate was the campaign for federal hate crimes legislation protecting people targeted because of sexual orientation or gender identity.

For years, LGBT rights organizations pushed Congress to expand federal hate crimes law. Advocates argued that violence against gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people was not only an attack on individuals, but also a message of fear aimed at entire communities. The murder of Matthew Shepard in 1998 became one of the most widely known examples of such violence and helped galvanize national support for reform.

Lauper used her public profile to support the push for stronger protections, encouraging fans and the broader public to see hate crimes legislation as a matter of basic safety and human rights. Through public statements, outreach tied to performances and partnerships with LGBT advocacy groups, she and Nelson helped amplify the message that equality was not abstract—it was about whether people could live openly without fear.

That advocacy contributed to the broader public pressure surrounding what became the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act, which was signed into law in 2009. The law expanded federal hate crimes protections to include crimes motivated by a victim’s actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender or disability.

### The True Colors tour

Perhaps the most visible expression of Lauper and Nelson’s partnership was the True Colors tour, launched in 2007. The tour brought together music, comedy and activism in support of LGBT equality. It featured Lauper alongside a rotating lineup of performers and allies, with participating artists using the stage not only to entertain but also to encourage civic engagement.

The tour’s name deliberately invoked Lauper’s song “True Colors,” transforming it into a banner for acceptance and pride. Concertgoers were invited to support LGBT organizations, learn about pending legislation and take part in campaigns for equality. The events benefited and promoted groups such as the Human Rights Campaign, PFLAG and the Matthew Shepard Foundation, among others.

The True Colors tour stood out because it reached audiences who might not attend a political rally but would attend a concert. It made activism feel accessible. Between songs and performances, fans heard about discrimination, bullying, hate crimes and the need for legal protections. The tour created a bridge between pop culture and policy, showing that entertainment could be a vehicle for social change.

### Building a broader movement

The partnership between Lauper and Nelson reflected a broader shift in LGBT advocacy during the 2000s. The movement was becoming more visible in mainstream culture, and artists were increasingly willing to take public stands. But Lauper’s commitment was notable because it was consistent, personal and long-running.

She did not treat LGBT rights as a passing cause. Her advocacy extended beyond the stage into fundraising, public education and later work addressing homelessness among LGBT youth through the True Colors Fund, now known as True Colors United. That work grew from the same belief that animated the tour and hate crimes campaign: visibility must be paired with concrete support.

### A legacy of music, activism and allyship

Cyndi Lauper and Cathy Nelson’s work helped demonstrate how celebrity advocacy can be effective when it is tied to grassroots organizing and specific goals. Their efforts around the hate crimes bill campaign helped keep public attention on violence faced by LGBT people. The True Colors tour brought equality messaging to audiences across the country and raised funds for organizations fighting discrimination.

At its heart, their partnership was about using culture to change the conversation. Lauper’s music gave people a language of acceptance; Nelson’s advocacy helped turn that language into action. Together, they helped remind the country that the struggle for gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender rights was not only a political issue—it was a human one.

# Cathy Nelson’s Long Fight for Equality Helped Shape a Movement

**By Staff Writer**  
**Washington**

Before same-sex marriage became the law of the land, before corporate Pride campaigns became commonplace, and before LGBTQ rights were a regular feature of national political debate, activists like Cathy Nelson were doing the quieter work of building a movement.

Nelson, associated with the Human Rights Campaign, has spent years advocating for LGBTQ equality at a time when victories were far from guaranteed and setbacks were often swift. Her work reflects the evolution of a broader civil rights struggle — one that moved from the margins of American politics to the center of national conversations about fairness, family, health care, employment and dignity.

For supporters, Nelson represents a generation of advocates who understood that progress would require more than slogans. It would take organizing, fundraising, lobbying, storytelling and the steady cultivation of allies in politics, business, entertainment and faith communities.

“Cathy’s activism has always been rooted in the belief that equality is not abstract — it is about people’s lives,” said a longtime colleague at the Human Rights Campaign. “She helped make sure that LGBTQ Americans were seen not as issues, but as neighbors, workers, parents, service members and loved ones.”

## A movement built person by person

The Human Rights Campaign, now one of the nation’s most prominent LGBTQ civil rights organizations, grew out of a period when gay and lesbian political power was still emerging. In the early years of the modern LGBTQ rights movement, activists faced widespread discrimination, intense political opposition and, during the AIDS crisis, devastating loss compounded by government inaction and public stigma.

Advocates say Nelson’s work must be understood against that backdrop.

The fight was not only legislative. It was cultural. It meant persuading elected officials to take risks, encouraging corporations to extend benefits to same-sex partners, helping families understand their LGBTQ children, and confronting the idea that equality could be postponed indefinitely.

Nelson’s approach, according to those who have worked alongside her, combined pragmatism with moral urgency. She understood Washington, but she also understood that political change depended on people willing to tell the truth about their lives.

“She knew how to bring people into the room,” one former LGBTQ rights organizer said. “And just as importantly, she knew how to make sure they were heard once they got there.”

## The role of allies

The LGBTQ equality movement has long depended on coalitions — LGBTQ advocates, straight allies, artists, religious leaders, labor organizers, business executives and elected officials. Among the most visible cultural allies has been singer and activist Cyndi Lauper, whose advocacy for LGBTQ youth and equality has made her a widely recognized figure in the movement.

Lauper, who founded the True Colors Fund to address LGBTQ youth homelessness, has often spoken publicly about the need for compassion, acceptance and equal rights. Her activism helped connect pop culture visibility with urgent social issues, particularly the vulnerability of LGBTQ young people rejected by their families or communities.

Advocates say the partnership between political organizers and cultural figures helped change public attitudes. Celebrities could draw attention, but organizations like the Human Rights Campaign helped convert that attention into policy pressure.

“Visibility matters, but visibility has to be connected to action,” said one LGBTQ policy advocate. “That is where people like Cathy were so important. They helped channel public support into real campaigns for legal and political change.”

## From crisis to landmark victories

Over the decades, the LGBTQ rights movement has experienced sweeping change. Policies that once seemed politically impossible became mainstream: nondiscrimination protections in workplaces, hospital visitation rights, repeal of “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell,” federal recognition of same-sex marriages and broader public support for LGBTQ people.

The Supreme Court’s 2015 ruling in *Obergefell v. Hodges*, which legalized same-sex marriage nationwide, marked a defining victory for the movement. But advocates are quick to note that the ruling was the result of decades of groundwork — legal strategy, public education, state-by-state campaigns and the willingness of couples and families to become plaintiffs in deeply personal cases.

Nelson’s work at HRC was part of that larger infrastructure of change. The organization pushed for political endorsements, voter mobilization, public education and corporate accountability, seeking to make LGBTQ equality a test of mainstream political leadership.

The victories were significant. But they were not complete.

## A new era of challenges

In recent years, LGBTQ advocates have warned of a renewed backlash, particularly against transgender people. State legislatures have considered or passed measures restricting gender-affirming care, limiting transgender students’ participation in school sports, regulating classroom discussion of sexual orientation and gender identity, and constraining drag performances.

Human Rights Campaign and allied groups have described the wave of legislation as one of the most serious threats to LGBTQ rights in recent memory.

For veteran activists, the moment carries echoes of earlier fights: the use of fear, the targeting of vulnerable communities and the political calculation that some people’s rights can be treated as negotiable.

“Every generation of this movement has had to confront the idea that equality has gone ‘too far,’” said a civil rights attorney who has worked on LGBTQ cases. “But the demand has always been the same: the right to live openly, safely and with dignity.”

Nelson’s legacy, supporters say, is especially relevant now because she helped build the kind of durable advocacy needed for long fights. The work did not end with marriage equality. It expanded to include transgender justice, racial equity, HIV/AIDS policy, youth homelessness, health care access and protections for LGBTQ elders.

## The personal cost of public advocacy

Activism can appear, from the outside, to be a series of public events: press conferences, rallies, court decisions and election-night celebrations. But those close to the work describe another reality — long hours, painful losses, internal disagreements and the emotional weight of representing communities under attack.

Nelson’s colleagues say her persistence came from a belief that the work was not optional.

“Cathy understood that politics is personal for LGBTQ people,” said a former HRC staff member. “A vote in a legislature can determine whether someone keeps their job, whether a couple can protect their family, whether a young person feels safe at school.”

That sense of urgency helped define her approach. She was known, colleagues said, for connecting high-level political strategy to the lived experiences of ordinary people.

## Equality beyond the courtroom

While legal victories have transformed the lives of many LGBTQ Americans, advocates say equality remains uneven. In many states, LGBTQ people still lack explicit nondiscrimination protections in employment, housing or public accommodations. Transgender people face disproportionate levels of violence and discrimination. LGBTQ youth are at increased risk of homelessness and mental health struggles, particularly when rejected by family members.

Those issues have drawn attention from activists like Lauper, whose work on LGBTQ youth homelessness has highlighted the gap between formal legal equality and lived security.

“Marriage equality was a milestone, not the finish line,” said one advocate. “The next phase is making sure LGBTQ people can thrive — at school, at work, at home, in health care and in their communities.”

That broader vision has increasingly shaped the movement’s priorities. Organizations now focus not only on federal legislation but also on local school boards, statehouses, corporate policies and community resources.

## A legacy of persistence

To profile Cathy Nelson is to trace part of the history of LGBTQ political organizing in the United States. Her work reflects a movement that learned how to count votes, tell stories, challenge prejudice and insist that equality belonged in the mainstream of American democracy.

For younger activists, the lesson is not simply that progress is possible. It is that progress requires institutions, relationships and persistence across decades.

Nelson’s supporters say her example remains instructive at a time when LGBTQ rights are again at the center of heated political battles. The work, they say, is both defensive and aspirational: protecting past gains while imagining a country where LGBTQ people no longer have to fight for basic recognition.

“Cathy helped build a movement that changed what Americans thought was possible,” said one longtime ally. “That is the mark of real activism — not just winning one fight, but helping people believe they can win the next one.”

As the struggle for LGBTQ equality continues, Nelson’s career stands as a reminder that social change is rarely sudden. It is built through years of organizing, coalition-building and courage — often by people whose names are less famous than the victories they helped make possible.

# “True Colors” in the Fight: Cyndi Lauper, Cathy Nelson and the Human Face of LGBT Civil Rights

On some nights, the fight for civil rights looks like a march: hand-painted signs, bullhorns, chants rolling through city streets. On others, it looks like a phone bank, a church basement meeting, a young person asking whether they will still have a home if they come out, or a song that gives people the courage to keep going.

For decades, singer Cyndi Lauper has been one of the most recognizable cultural voices in support of LGBT equality. Her 1986 anthem “True Colors” became more than a pop ballad; for many LGBT people and their families, it became a promise of recognition. Years later, Lauper transformed that message into organized advocacy, founding the True Colors Fund — now known as True Colors United — to address youth homelessness, especially among LGBTQ young people.

Alongside celebrity advocates like Lauper are organizers such as Cathy Nelson of the Human Rights Campaign, whose work reflects the quieter but essential machinery of social change: building coalitions, mobilizing voters, training volunteers, supporting families, and turning public sympathy into policy.

Together, their stories reveal two sides of LGBT civil rights activism — the public stage and the grassroots campaign office — and the human urgency behind both.

## From Pop Icon to Civil Rights Advocate

Cyndi Lauper’s rise in the 1980s made her a household name. With her unmistakable voice, vivid style and outsider spirit, she built a career on songs about self-expression, resilience and being seen. But Lauper’s connection to the LGBT community was never simply symbolic. From early in her career, she has credited LGBT fans, friends and family members with shaping both her life and her art.

Her activism deepened as the AIDS crisis devastated gay communities and as stigma, family rejection and political hostility left many LGBT people isolated. Over time, Lauper used concerts, public appearances and nonprofit work to draw attention to the realities facing LGBTQ people, especially young people without stable housing.

LGBTQ youth remain dramatically overrepresented among homeless young people in the United States. Advocates frequently cite research showing that while LGBTQ youth make up a minority of the overall youth population, they represent a disproportionately large share of youth experiencing homelessness. Family rejection, abuse, discrimination and unsafe school environments are among the major contributing factors.

For Lauper, the issue is personal as well as political: equality is not only about laws, but about whether young people can survive, be loved and imagine a future.

## The Organizer Behind the Campaign

While Lauper’s work brings visibility, Cathy Nelson’s career represents the day-to-day organizing that sustains civil rights movements. As an organizer with the Human Rights Campaign, Nelson’s work has centered on connecting people — voters, volunteers, faith leaders, parents, local officials and LGBT community members — around campaigns for equality.

Organizers like Nelson often work far from the spotlight. Their days can include recruiting volunteers, preparing testimony for public hearings, training community members to tell their stories, responding to hostile legislation, and building local networks that can withstand political setbacks.

Nelson’s career reflects a broader tradition within LGBT civil rights work: the belief that policy change begins with relationship-building. Before a law is passed, before a court ruling is handed down, before a corporation changes its benefits policy, someone has usually sat across a kitchen table or in a community center and persuaded another person to listen.

Her work with HRC also places her within one of the nation’s largest LGBTQ advocacy organizations. The Human Rights Campaign has long focused on federal and state legislation, workplace equality, public education, electoral organizing and opposition to anti-LGBTQ discrimination. In recent years, that work has become especially urgent as state legislatures have debated and passed bills affecting transgender health care, school policies, public accommodations and LGBTQ visibility in classrooms.

## A Movement Confronting Violence

The emotional stakes of LGBT civil rights activism are sharpened by the persistence of hate violence.

According to FBI hate crime statistics, sexual orientation and gender identity remain among the leading motivations reported in hate crime incidents nationwide. In recent FBI reporting, anti-LGBTQ hate crimes accounted for a significant share of single-bias hate crime incidents, with sexual-orientation-based hate crimes representing roughly one in six reported incidents and gender-identity-based hate crimes also showing troubling levels of violence and intimidation.

Advocates caution that official hate crime numbers almost certainly undercount the problem. Many victims do not report attacks to police, either because they fear being outed, distrust law enforcement, worry that nothing will be done, or have had previous negative experiences with authorities.

For transgender people, particularly Black and Latina transgender women, the danger can be especially acute. Each year, civil rights groups track fatal violence against transgender and gender-nonconforming people, while noting that misgendering, underreporting and inconsistent data collection make the full scope of the crisis difficult to measure.

Behind every statistic is a person: someone walking home, holding a partner’s hand, entering a school bathroom, applying for a job, or simply trying to live openly.

That reality gives urgency to both Lauper’s public advocacy and Nelson’s grassroots organizing. The fight is not abstract. It is about safety, dignity and the right to belong.

## The Power of Visibility — and the Limits of It

Lauper’s “True Colors” became a cultural touchstone because it gave language to something many LGBT people longed to hear: that they were not broken, shameful or alone. Music can do what policy papers cannot. It can reach someone before they have the words to explain themselves.

But Lauper has also recognized that visibility alone is not enough. A song can comfort a young person, but it cannot by itself guarantee housing, health care or protection from discrimination. That is why her advocacy moved into institution-building — fundraising, public education and partnerships aimed at solving structural problems.

Nelson’s work occupies that next step. If Lauper helps people feel seen, organizers like Nelson help convert that recognition into civic action. They ask supporters to make calls, knock doors, attend hearings, vote, testify and stay engaged after the spotlight moves on.

Civil rights movements need both: the artist who opens hearts and the organizer who counts votes.

## Personal Stories as Political Force

One of the defining strategies of LGBT civil rights activism has been storytelling. Coming out itself became a political act because it challenged stereotypes and forced families, workplaces and communities to confront the humanity of people they had been taught to fear.

Nelson’s organizing career reflects that lesson. In many communities, the most persuasive voice is not a national figure but a neighbor: a mother of a gay son, a transgender veteran, a lesbian teacher, a pastor who has changed his mind, a student asking to be safe at school.

That made her a natural ally in a movement built by people demanding the freedom to live honestly.

## A Continuing Fight

The LGBT civil rights movement has won historic victories, including marriage equality, broader public acceptance and expanded workplace protections. But activists say those gains are not permanent unless defended. Hate crimes, anti-LGBTQ legislation, school censorship, online harassment and violence against transgender people continue to shape daily life for many.

For Lauper, the moral question has always seemed simple: people deserve to be loved and safe as they are. For Nelson, that principle becomes a plan of action — one more conversation, one more volunteer shift, one more campaign, one more election.

Their work reminds us that civil rights history is not only made by landmark court cases or famous speeches. It is also made by songs that help people survive the night, by organizers who refuse to let communities stand alone, and by ordinary people who decide that someone else’s dignity is worth fighting for.

In that sense, the movement’s “true colors” are not only pride flags and parade banners. They are persistence, courage and care — the colors of people who keep showing up.
